3|HWP-IUL-2024-7290 Policy and Associated Index Accounts|"# HWP-IUL-2024-7290 Policy and Associated Index Accounts

The community centers on the HWP-IUL-2024-7290 life insurance policy, which incorporates four primary investment accounts: S&P 500 Index, NASDAQ-100 Index, Global Diversified Index, and Fixed Account. These accounts are interconnected through policy features such as the point-to-point method, cap rates, participation rates, and floor rates. The policy’s current allocation is 50% in the S&P 500 Index, 30% in the NASDAQ-100 Index, and 20% in the Fixed Account, with Jessica Lynn Thompson identified as a policyholder. The community is governed by a set of guaranteed rates that protect minimum performance thresholds across all index accounts.

## HWP-IUL-2024-7290 as the central policy entity

The HWP-IUL-2024-7290 policy is the central entity in this community, serving as the overarching structure that integrates multiple investment accounts and policy features. It is explicitly linked to the S&P 500 Index Account, NASDAQ-100 Index Account, Global Diversified Index Account, and Fixed Account, each of which functions as an investment option within the policy. The policy’s structure enables variable interest crediting based on market performance while providing certain guarantees. This central role makes HWP-IUL-2024-7290 the primary node through which all other entities are connected and evaluated [Data: Relationships (10, 19, 28, 36); Entities (4, 5, 6, 7, 20, 21)]

## S&P 500 Index Account as the primary investment driver

The S&P 500 Index Account is the largest component of the policy’s investment allocation, representing 50% of the current distribution. It is tied to the performance of the S&P 500 stock market index using the point-to-point method, with a cap rate of 10.5%, a participation rate of 100%, and a floor rate of 0%. These parameters allow the account to benefit fully from market gains up to the cap, while protecting the policyholder from losses. The account’s performance is directly dependent on the beginning and ending index values over the crediting period, which are key inputs in the interest crediting formula [Data: Entities (4), Relationships (10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18); Current Allocation (20)]

## NASDAQ-100 and Global Diversified Index Accounts provide market exposure

The NASDAQ-100 Index Account and Global Diversified Index Account serve as secondary investment vehicles within the policy, contributing 30% and 20% respectively to the current allocation. The NASDAQ-100 Index Account uses the same point-to-point method and has a cap rate of 9.0% and a participation rate of 100%, offering exposure to technology and growth-oriented equities. The Global Diversified Index Account, with a cap rate of 8.5% and 100% participation, provides international market diversification. Both accounts are subject to the same floor rate of 0%, ensuring no negative interest crediting. These accounts collectively enhance the policy’s potential for growth while maintaining risk mitigation through guaranteed minimums [Data: Entities (5, 6); Relationships (19, 28); Current Allocation (20)]

## Fixed Account ensures stable, guaranteed returns

The Fixed Account is a guaranteed interest account that earns a stable 3.0% annual return, independent of market fluctuations. It is allocated 20% of the policy’s funds and serves as a risk-mitigating component, providing predictable returns. Unlike index accounts, it has no caps or floors, meaning the full 3.0% is credited regardless of market conditions. This account is particularly valuable in volatile market environments, offering a reliable base for the policy’s overall performance. Its inclusion in the policy structure reflects a balanced approach to risk and return [Data: Entities (7); Relationships (36); Current Allocation (20)]

## Point-to-point method drives interest crediting

The point-to-point method is the core calculation mechanism used to determine interest crediting for all index accounts. It measures the percentage change in the index value from the beginning to the end of the crediting period, typically annual. This method ensures that gains are calculated based on the full period’s performance, rather than daily or monthly fluctuations. The method is applied consistently across the S&P 500, NASDAQ-100, and Global Diversified Index Accounts, making it a foundational feature of the policy’s investment engine. The accuracy of the beginning and ending index values is critical to the final interest crediting outcome [Data: Entities (9); Relationships (11, 17, 18)]

## Cap, participation, and floor rates define performance boundaries

The policy’s index accounts are governed by three key performance parameters: cap rate, participation rate, and floor rate. The cap rate sets the maximum interest that can be credited—10.5% for the S&P 500, 9.0% for NASDAQ-100, and 8.5% for the Global Diversified Index. The participation rate determines the percentage of index gains credited to the policyholder, currently 100% across all index accounts, meaning full upside potential is captured up to the cap. The floor rate of 0% ensures that the policyholder will not lose money due to market declines, providing downside protection. These features collectively shape the risk-return profile of the policy [Data: Entities (14, 16, 15); Relationships (12, 13, 14)]

The heavy weighting in the S&P 500 provides exposure to broad U.S. equity markets, while the NASDAQ-100 adds concentration in technology and innovation sectors. The policy’s design enables long-term wealth accumulation and estate planning benefits, particularly for individuals seeking tax-advantaged growth. 3|HWP-IUL-2024-7290 Policy and Associated Index Accounts|"# HWP-IUL-2024-7290 Policy and Associated Index Accounts

The community centers on the HWP-IUL-2024-7290 life insurance policy, which incorporates four primary investment accounts: S&P 500 Index, NASDAQ-100 Index, Global Diversified Index, and Fixed Account. These accounts are interconnected through policy features such as the point-to-point method, cap rates, participation rates, and floor rates. The policy’s current allocation is 50% in the S&P 500 Index, 30% in the NASDAQ-100 Index, and 20% in the Fixed Account, with Jessica Lynn Thompson identified as a policyholder. The community is governed by a set of guaranteed rates that protect minimum performance thresholds across all index accounts.

## HWP-IUL-2024-7290 as the central policy entity

The HWP-IUL-2024-7290 policy is the central entity in this community, serving as the overarching structure that integrates multiple investment accounts and policy features. It is explicitly linked to the S&P 500 Index Account, NASDAQ-100 Index Account, Global Diversified Index Account, and Fixed Account, each of which functions as an investment option within the policy. The policy’s structure enables variable interest crediting based on market performance while providing certain guarantees. This central role makes HWP-IUL-2024-7290 the primary node through which all other entities are connected and evaluated [Data: Relationships (10, 19, 28, 36); Entities (4, 5, 6, 7, 20, 21)]

## S&P 500 Index Account as the primary investment driver

The S&P 500 Index Account is the largest component of the policy’s investment allocation, representing 50% of the current distribution. It is tied to the performance of the S&P 500 stock market index using the point-to-point method, with a cap rate of 10.5%, a participation rate of 100%, and a floor rate of 0%. These parameters allow the account to benefit fully from market gains up to the cap, while protecting the policyholder from losses. The account’s performance is directly dependent on the beginning and ending index values over the crediting period, which are key inputs in the interest crediting formula [Data: Entities (4), Relationships (10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18); Current Allocation (20)]

## NASDAQ-100 and Global Diversified Index Accounts provide market exposure

The NASDAQ-100 Index Account and Global Diversified Index Account serve as secondary investment vehicles within the policy, contributing 30% and 20% respectively to the current allocation. The NASDAQ-100 Index Account uses the same point-to-point method and has a cap rate of 9.0% and a participation rate of 100%, offering exposure to technology and growth-oriented equities. The Global Diversified Index Account, with a cap rate of 8.5% and 100% participation, provides international market diversification. Both accounts are subject to the same floor rate of 0%, ensuring no negative interest crediting. These accounts collectively enhance the policy’s potential for growth while maintaining risk mitigation through guaranteed minimums [Data: Entities (5, 6); Relationships (19, 28); Current Allocation (20)]

## Fixed Account ensures stable, guaranteed returns

The Fixed Account is a guaranteed interest account that earns a stable 3.0% annual return, independent of market fluctuations. It is allocated 20% of the policy’s funds and serves as a risk-mitigating component, providing predictable returns. Unlike index accounts, it has no caps or floors, meaning the full 3.0% is credited regardless of market conditions. This account is particularly valuable in volatile market environments, offering a reliable base for the policy’s overall performance. Its inclusion in the policy structure reflects a balanced approach to risk and return [Data: Entities (7); Relationships (36); Current Allocation (20)]

## Point-to-point method drives interest crediting

The point-to-point method is the core calculation mechanism used to determine interest crediting for all index accounts. It measures the percentage change in the index value from the beginning to the end of the crediting period, typically annual. This method ensures that gains are calculated based on the full period’s performance, rather than daily or monthly fluctuations. The method is applied consistently across the S&P 500, NASDAQ-100, and Global Diversified Index Accounts, making it a foundational feature of the policy’s investment engine. 1|Jessica Lynn Thompson's Life Insurance Policy Community|"# Jessica Lynn Thompson's Life Insurance Policy Community

The community centers around Jessica Lynn Thompson and her life insurance policy, which is governed by a structured set of financial mechanisms including index crediting, policy anniversary reviews, reallocations, and death benefit options. Key entities such as the S&P 500 Index, CAP, FLOOR, and participation rates influence interest crediting, while the policy anniversary serves as a recurring administrative milestone. The policyholder has selected a level death benefit with lower charges and the right to reallocate investments annually, with constraints on changes and requirements for evidence of insurability when modifying coverage.

## Policy Anniversary as the central administrative cycle

The POLICY ANNIVERSARY is a recurring annual event that serves as the cornerstone of the policy’s lifecycle, triggering multiple critical functions including interest crediting, investment reallocation, and death benefit review. This date provides a structured, predictable framework for policy management, ensuring alignment between market conditions and the policyholder’s financial goals. The annual review allows for adjustments to investment allocations and evaluation of death benefit options, maintaining the policy’s responsiveness to both external market dynamics and internal personal circumstances. This recurring event is essential for transparency and ongoing engagement between the policyholder and insurer [Data: Entities (10), Relationships (39, 61, 62, 63, +more)].

## Index crediting mechanism tied to S&P 500 performance

The INDEX CREDITING mechanism determines the interest credited to the policy based on the performance of the S&P 500 Index, which serves as the benchmark for calculating gains. The S&P 500 Index tracks 500 large-cap U.S. companies and is used to measure the percentage change that influences the interest credited to the policy. This mechanism allows policyholders to benefit from market growth while being protected from losses through predefined safeguards. The use of the S&P 500 ensures a widely recognized and stable reference point for performance evaluation [Data: Entities (27, 28), Relationships (50, 51, 52, 53, +more)].

## Interest crediting is constrained by caps, floors, and participation rates

The interest credited to the policy is not directly proportional to the S&P 500’s performance due to structural limits. The CAP sets a maximum interest rate that can be credited, protecting the insurer from excessive payouts even if the index performs exceptionally well. Conversely, the FLOOR ensures that the interest credited never falls below 0%, providing downside protection to the policyholder during market downturns. The PARTICIPATION RATE determines the proportion of the index’s gain that is applied to the interest credited, directly affecting the final amount. These parameters collectively shape the risk-return profile of the policy, balancing potential gains with insurer risk management [Data: Entities (29, 30, 28), Relationships (51, 52, 53, +more)].

## Jessica Lynn Thompson exercises reallocation rights annually

Jessica Lynn Thompson has the right to reallocate her policy’s investments annually, with up to four free changes per year and a $25 fee for additional changes. This feature, known as REALLOCATIONS, allows her to adjust her investment exposure in response to evolving financial goals or market conditions. The reallocation capability is tied to the POLICY ANNIVERSARY, which serves as the annual window for such changes. This flexibility supports dynamic portfolio management and enables the policyholder to maintain alignment with personal risk tolerance and long-term objectives. The ability to modify allocations annually enhances the policy’s adaptability and engagement [Data: Entities (22, 10), Relationships (9, 39, +more)].

## Death benefit options are structured with trade-offs in cost and benefit

The DEATH BENEFIT OPTIONS provide policyholders with two primary choices: OPTION 1 - LEVEL DEATH BENEFIT, which offers a fixed $500,000 benefit with lower ongoing charges, and OPTION 2 - INCREASING DEATH BENEFIT, which grows with the account value but incurs higher charges. Jessica Lynn Thompson has selected the level option, which provides stability and cost efficiency. However, switching to the increasing option or increasing coverage under it requires submission of EVIDENCE OF INSURABILITY, a formal assessment of the policyholder’s current health and insurability. This requirement ensures that the insurer maintains risk control when altering coverage terms. The trade-off between cost and benefit is central to the policy’s design and decision-making process [Data: Entities (37, 38, 39, 58), Relationships (61, 62, 63, +more)].

## Crediting calculation depends on index performance and policy parameters

The CREDITING CALCULATION process determines the annual interest credited to the policy by analyzing the change in the index over the crediting period, using the ending index value as a key input. This calculation is performed annually on the POLICY ANNIVERSARY and incorporates the policy’s specific parameters, including the CAP, FLOOR, and PARTICIPATION RATE. The final interest amount is derived from the index’s percentage change, adjusted by the participation rate, and capped at the maximum allowed rate. This structured approach ensures consistency and predictability in interest crediting while protecting the insurer from market volatility. The calculation is a critical technical component that directly affects the policy’s growth and value [Data: Entities (23, 10), Relationships (39, 48, 51, 52, 53, +more)].

## Evidence of insurability required for coverage changes

EVIDENCE OF INSURABILITY is a mandatory requirement when a policyholder seeks to increase coverage or switch from the level death benefit to the increasing option. This requirement ensures that the policyholder still qualifies for additional life insurance protection based on current health and financial standing. The need for evidence of insurability introduces a formal review process that may involve medical exams or underwriting assessments. This safeguard protects the insurer from adverse selection and ensures that coverage changes are made responsibly. For Jessica Lynn Thompson, this means that any future expansion of benefits would require a formal application and approval process [Data: Entities (58), Relationships (63, +more)]."

    • Interest credited: 0% (no loss)

    On each policy anniversary, we calculate:

                       (subject to Cap and Floor)

    • Floor protects at 0%
    • Interest credited: 0% (no loss)

    worst case is 0% interest for that year.

1|Jessica Lynn Thompson's Life Insurance Policy Community|"# Jessica Lynn Thompson's Life Insurance Policy Community

The community centers around Jessica Lynn Thompson and her life insurance policy, which is governed by a structured set of financial mechanisms including index crediting, policy anniversary reviews, reallocations, and death benefit options. Key entities such as the S&P 500 Index, CAP, FLOOR, and participation rates influence interest crediting, while the policy anniversary serves as a recurring administrative milestone. The policyholder has selected a level death benefit with lower charges and the right to reallocate investments annually, with constraints on changes and requirements for evidence of insurability when modifying coverage.

## Policy Anniversary as the central administrative cycle

The POLICY ANNIVERSARY is a recurring annual event that serves as the cornerstone of the policy’s lifecycle, triggering multiple critical functions including interest crediting, investment reallocation, and death benefit review. This date provides a structured, predictable framework for policy management, ensuring alignment between market conditions and the policyholder’s financial goals. The annual review allows for adjustments to investment allocations and evaluation of death benefit options, maintaining the policy’s responsiveness to both external market dynamics and internal personal circumstances. This recurring event is essential for transparency and ongoing engagement between the policyholder and insurer [Data: Entities (10), Relationships (39, 61, 62, 63, +more)].

## Index crediting mechanism tied to S&P 500 performance

The INDEX CREDITING mechanism determines the interest credited to the policy based on the performance of the S&P 500 Index, which serves as the benchmark for calculating gains. The S&P 500 Index tracks 500 large-cap U.S. companies and is used to measure the percentage change that influences the interest credited to the policy. This mechanism allows policyholders to benefit from market growth while being protected from losses through predefined safeguards. The use of the S&P 500 ensures a widely recognized and stable reference point for performance evaluation [Data: Entities (27, 28), Relationships (50, 51, 52, 53, +more)].

## Interest crediting is constrained by caps, floors, and participation rates

The interest credited to the policy is not directly proportional to the S&P 500’s performance due to structural limits. The CAP sets a maximum interest rate that can be credited, protecting the insurer from excessive payouts even if the index performs exceptionally well. Conversely, the FLOOR ensures that the interest credited never falls below 0%, providing downside protection to the policyholder during market downturns. The PARTICIPATION RATE determines the proportion of the index’s gain that is applied to the interest credited, directly affecting the final amount. These parameters collectively shape the risk-return profile of the policy, balancing potential gains with insurer risk management [Data: Entities (29, 30, 28), Relationships (51, 52, 53, +more)].

## Jessica Lynn Thompson exercises reallocation rights annually

Jessica Lynn Thompson has the right to reallocate her policy’s investments annually, with up to four free changes per year and a $25 fee for additional changes. This feature, known as REALLOCATIONS, allows her to adjust her investment exposure in response to evolving financial goals or market conditions. The reallocation capability is tied to the POLICY ANNIVERSARY, which serves as the annual window for such changes. This flexibility supports dynamic portfolio management and enables the policyholder to maintain alignment with personal risk tolerance and long-term objectives. The ability to modify allocations annually enhances the policy’s adaptability and engagement [Data: Entities (22, 10), Relationships (9, 39, +more)].

## Death benefit options are structured with trade-offs in cost and benefit

The DEATH BENEFIT OPTIONS provide policyholders with two primary choices: OPTION 1 - LEVEL DEATH BENEFIT, which offers a fixed $500,000 benefit with lower ongoing charges, and OPTION 2 - INCREASING DEATH BENEFIT, which grows with the account value but incurs higher charges. Jessica Lynn Thompson has selected the level option, which provides stability and cost efficiency. However, switching to the increasing option or increasing coverage under it requires submission of EVIDENCE OF INSURABILITY, a formal assessment of the policyholder’s current health and insurability. This requirement ensures that the insurer maintains risk control when altering coverage terms. The trade-off between cost and benefit is central to the policy’s design and decision-making process [Data: Entities (37, 38, 39, 58), Relationships (61, 62, 63, +more)].

## Crediting calculation depends on index performance and policy parameters

The CREDITING CALCULATION process determines the annual interest credited to the policy by analyzing the change in the index over the crediting period, using the ending index value as a key input. This calculation is performed annually on the POLICY ANNIVERSARY and incorporates the policy’s specific parameters, including the CAP, FLOOR, and PARTICIPATION RATE. The final interest amount is derived from the index’s percentage change, adjusted by the participation rate, and capped at the maximum allowed rate. This structured approach ensures consistency and predictability in interest crediting while protecting the insurer from market volatility. The calculation is a critical technical component that directly affects the policy’s growth and value [Data: Entities (23, 10), Relationships (39, 48, 51, 52, 53, +more)].

## Evidence of insurability required for coverage changes

EVIDENCE OF INSURABILITY is a mandatory requirement when a policyholder seeks to increase coverage or switch from the level death benefit to the increasing option. This requirement ensures that the policyholder still qualifies for additional life insurance protection based on current health and financial standing. The need for evidence of insurability introduces a formal review process that may involve medical exams or underwriting assessments. This safeguard protects the insurer from adverse selection and ensures that coverage changes are made responsibly. For Jessica Lynn Thompson, this means that any future expansion of benefits would require a formal application and approval process [Data: Entities (58), Relationships (63, +more)]."

ARTICLE 3 - HOW INDEX CREDITING WORKS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
3.1 CREDITING CALCULATION:
    On each policy anniversary, we calculate:
    
    Index % Change = (Ending Index Value - Starting Index Value) 
                     ÷ Starting Index Value
    
    Interest Credited = Index % Change × Participation Rate
                       (subject to Cap and Floor)

3.2 EXAMPLE:
    Assume S&P 500 Index:
    • Started at 4,000
    • Ended at 4,600
    • Gain: 15%
    • With 100% participation and 10.5% cap
    • Interest credited: 10.5% (capped)
    
    If index declined 5%:
    • Floor protects at 0%
    • Interest credited: 0% (no loss)

3.3 CRITICAL: You never lose money due to market decline. The 
    worst case is 0% interest for that year.

    coverage to age 100 based on current assumptions.

4.3 You may skip premium payments as long as account value is 
    sufficient to cover monthly deductions.

    expenses.

The community centers on the HWP-IUL-2024-7290 life insurance policy, which incorporates four primary investment accounts: S&P 500 Index, NASDAQ-100 Index, Global Diversified Index, and Fixed Account.                        (subject to Cap and Floor)

    • Floor protects at 0%
    • Interest credited: 0% (no loss)

    worst case is 0% interest for that year.

The community centers on the HWP-IUL-2024-7290 life insurance policy, which incorporates four primary investment accounts: S&P 500 Index, NASDAQ-100 Index, Global Diversified Index, and Fixed Account. ## HWP-IUL-2024-7290 as the central policy entity

The HWP-IUL-2024-7290 policy is the central entity in this community, serving as the overarching structure that integrates multiple investment accounts and policy features. The Fixed Account is a guaranteed interest account that earns a stable 3.0% annual return, independent of market fluctuations. It is allocated 20% of the policy’s funds and serves as a risk-mitigating component, providing predictable returns. Unlike index accounts, it has no caps or floors, meaning the full 3.0% is credited regardless of market conditions. This account is particularly valuable in volatile market environments, offering a reliable base for the policy’s overall performance. Its inclusion in the policy structure reflects a balanced approach to risk and return [Data: Entities (7); Relationships (36); Current Allocation (20)]

The point-to-point method is the core calculation mechanism used to determine interest crediting for all index accounts. It measures the percentage change in the index value from the beginning to the end of the crediting period, typically annual. This method ensures that gains are calculated based on the full period’s performance, rather than daily or monthly fluctuations. The method is applied consistently across the S&P 500, NASDAQ-100, and Global Diversified Index Accounts, making it a foundational feature of the policy’s investment engine. ARTICLE 3 - HOW INDEX CREDITING WORKS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
3.1 CREDITING CALCULATION:
    On each policy anniversary, we calculate:
    
    Index % Change = (Ending Index Value - Starting Index Value) 
                     ÷ Starting Index Value
    
    Interest Credited = Index % Change × Participation Rate
                       (subject to Cap and Floor)

3.2 EXAMPLE:
    Assume S&P 500 Index:
    • Started at 4,000
    • Ended at 4,600
    • Gain: 15%
    • With 100% participation and 10.5% cap
    • Interest credited: 10.5% (capped)
    
    If index declined 5%:
    • Floor protects at 0%
    • Interest credited: 0% (no loss)

3.3 CRITICAL: You never lose money due to market decline. The 
    worst case is 0% interest for that year.
